text: lar depression.2,3,5,7 Antidepressants 373 The symbol † denotes a preparation no longer actively marketed The symbol  denotes a substance whose use may be restricted in certain sports (see p.vii) Once the acute phase has been brought under control, drug therapy should be continued until the patient is thought unlikely to suffer a relapse; this might entail maintaining treatment for several months.2,5,15 When full remission has been achieved treatment should be gradually stopped over several weeks unless long-term treatment is planned (see below). Antipsychotics and antidepressants are usual- ly stopped unless residual symptoms persist. Some guidelines2,5 recommend that long-term treatment should be started after a single episode of mania although others generally wait until a patient has had at least 2 man- ic episodes.6 Lithium is often the drug of choice for the long-term treatment of bipolar disorder.2,3,5 It reduces the risk of relapse, particularly mania,2 although its prophylac- tic effects on depression are less obvious.16 Long-term lithium treatment has also been associated with an anti-sui- cide effect.2,15 Other treatment options include valproate, lamotrigine (particularly if bipolar depression is a burden), olanzapine, and possibly carbamazepine or oxcar- bazepine.2,3,5,6,9 Combination therapy may be necessary in those who fail on monotherapy; ECT and clozapine have also been tried in treatment-resistant patients.2,9 However, it is usual practice for patients to continue with their acute treatment, given at the same doses, if effective.2,5,6 There is no consensus on the appropriate duration of long- term treatment and in some patients with severe disorders it may be necessary to continue treatment indefinitely. 1.
